name: LQER (low-rank quantization error reconstruction)
activation_scheme: 8-bit activations. Weights are represented as quantized values PLUS a low-rank correction: an activation-induced scale matrix drives the singular-value distribution of the quantization error towards a favourable shape, letting a truncated SVD absorb the residual. Claimed to work without knowledge distillation, grid search, or gradient-based iterative optimization.
kernels: Reference implementation open-sourced (ChengZhang-98/lqer). Notable: the computation pattern avoids Scatter/Gather from irregular high-precision weight locations, unlike Atom.
quality_delta: From the abstract: 'near-lossless W4A8 quantization on various LLMs and downstream tasks' without knowledge distillation, grid search, or gradient iterative optimization; near-lossless on six downstream tasks while using 1.36x fewer hardware resources than the leading state-of-the-art method. No per-task numbers in the abstract; none recorded.
notes: GROUP SIZE LEFT NULL 2026-10-04. LEFT NULL 2026-10-04. The paper says only 'quantizing other weights to 4-bit grouped fixed-point' - it states that grouping is used but never publishes the group width in the text available here, and the 1% salient weights go to FP16 rather than to a wider grid. A plausible 128 would be a guess. Enum mismatch: 'gptq' is the closest enum since the base grid is a grouped weight quantizer like GPTQ, but LQER is not a GPTQ variant - it adds a low-rank term to the weight representation, which is a different tradeoff (slightly more memory, much less error) than GPTQ's error-compensation across columns. That 'mixed precision with a structural rather than a sparsity-based split' idea is the same family as Atom and Macaron. Note the activations here are 8-bit, so LQER is W4A8, not W4A4 - it does not need rotations because 8-bit activations have no outliers severe enough to require removing.
